definition: The notes of a chord played one after another instead of together.
A short solo passage where the rest of the orchestra stops and one player or singer is free to linger.
One instrument plays a melody and another follows a moment later with the same melody, like a round.
Slow, hymn-like music that moves in solemn chords.
A closing section added to the end of a movement.
Tapping the strings with the wooden back of the bow, which makes a dry, clicking sound.
Getting gradually louder.
The middle stage of sonata form, where the themes are broken up, combined and pushed through different keys.
A medieval chant from the Mass for the dead. Composers quote it as a symbol of death.
A string section split into two or more groups, each playing a different line.
The first stage of sonata form, where the main themes are introduced. It is often repeated.
A passage that starts like a fugue, with instruments entering one by one on the same tune, without being a full fugue.
A piece or section in which one tune enters in each voice in turn and is woven against itself.
A continuous slide from one note to another.
“Fixed idea”: Berlioz’s term for a melody that represents a person and returns throughout a piece.
A rustic Austrian country dance in three beats, a slower, heavier ancestor of the waltz.
The kind of key that generally sounds bright or settled. Its darker counterpart is the minor.
An elegant 18th-century dance in three beats, used as the third movement of Classical symphonies.
The smallest musical idea, just a few notes, from which a theme is built.
Played with a small device on the instrument that softens and veils the sound.
A solo instrumental part that is essential and prominent throughout a movement.
A form in which a short theme repeats over and over while the music around it keeps changing.
A single note held or repeated, usually in the bass, while the harmony changes above it.
Plucking the strings of a string instrument with the finger instead of using the bow.
Instrumental music that tells a story or depicts a scene described by the composer.
The last stage of sonata form, where the opening themes return.
Music that imitates the rhythm of speech, free and unmeasured.
A form in which one main theme keeps returning between contrasting episodes.
A fast, energetic movement, usually third in a symphony. The word means “joke”, though the mood is often far from funny.
A three-stage structure: themes are introduced (exposition), worked and set against each other (development), and brought back (recapitulation).
Accents placed off the main beats, which makes the rhythm feel as if it is floating or pulling against the pulse.
The contrasting middle section of a minuet or scherzo, usually gentler.
Everyone playing the same notes at the same time.
A repeat of a theme in which something is changed: the decoration, the rhythm, the harmony or the instruments.
